Theory.theory: A sliding window maintains a contiguous interval [left,right]. Fixed-size windows add one entry and remove one each step. Variable windows expand right and shrink left until a monotone validity condition holds. Distinct-count, zero-count and nonnegative sums have useful monotonicity; arbitrary signed sums do not. For an at-most-k count, all suffixes of a valid window ending at right are valid, adding right-left+1. Exactly k often equals atMost(k)-atMost(k-1). A two-pointer proof counts total pointer moves: each pointer advances at most n times, even when a while loop is nested inside a for loop.

Maximum Points You Can Obtain from Cards.problem: Take exactly k cards, one at a time from either end, maximizing score. Values may be negative.
Maximum Points You Can Obtain from Cards.approach: Every choice takes a prefix of length k-j and a suffix of length j. Enumerate all j=0..k, updating by replacing one left card with one right card.
Maximum Points You Can Obtain from Cards.trace: Scores for three cards: left 1+2+3=6; then 1+2+1=4; 1+6+1=8; 5+6+1=12.
Maximum Points You Can Obtain from Cards.pitfalls: k=0 returns zero. For k=n each candidate still counts each card exactly once.
Maximum Points You Can Obtain from Cards.alternatives: Alternatively subtract the minimum sum window of size n-k from total in O(n) time.

Longest Substring Without Repeating Char.problem: Return the longest substring length with all UTF-16 characters distinct.
Longest Substring Without Repeating Char.approach: When character c repeats inside the window, move left past its previous occurrence. Never move left backwards. The maintained interval contains no repeated character.
Longest Substring Without Repeating Char.trace: abc reaches length 3; repeated a moves left to 1, preserving unique bca.
Longest Substring Without Repeating Char.pitfalls: For abba, last a is outside the current window; max(left,previous+1) prevents an incorrect backward move.
Longest Substring Without Repeating Char.alternatives: Enumerate starts and expand until a repeat in O(n²) time.

Max Consecutive Ones III.problem: For binary input, flip at most k zeros to ones; maximize the consecutive-one length.
Max Consecutive Ones III.approach: A window is valid exactly when it has <=k zeros. Expanding adds at most one zero; shrink until valid, then compare length.
Max Consecutive Ones III.trace: Window [0,0,1,1,1,1] contains two zeros and reaches length 6.
Max Consecutive Ones III.pitfalls: k=0 reduces to ordinary consecutive ones. Contract assumes all entries are binary.

Fruit Into Baskets.problem: Collect the longest contiguous run using at most two fruit types.
Fruit Into Baskets.approach: Keep a frequency map for the window. Shrink until there are no more than two keys; counts are required to know when a type fully leaves.
Fruit Into Baskets.complexity: Expected O(n) time; O(1) type-map space since at most three types are temporarily stored.
Fruit Into Baskets.trace: [1,2,1,2] fits two types; adding 3 forces the window to shrink.
Fruit Into Baskets.pitfalls: This asks for a contiguous interval, not the two most frequent types in the whole array.

Longest Substring With At Most K Distinc.problem: Return maximum substring length using at most k distinct UTF-16 characters.
Longest Substring With At Most K Distinc.approach: Maintain counts, shrinking only while type count exceeds k. After shrinking, current left is the earliest feasible start for this right endpoint.
Longest Substring With At Most K Distinc.trace: ece has two types and length 3; b requires dropping through the first c.
Longest Substring With At Most K Distinc.pitfalls: Remove zero-count keys, otherwise map.size does not reflect active types.

Longest Repeating Character Replacement.problem: Uppercase A..Z only. Change at most k characters to make a substring consist of one repeated character.
Longest Repeating Character Replacement.approach: The replacements required are window length minus the largest frequency. Recompute the exact maximum over 26 counters when shrinking; every kept window is actually feasible.
Longest Repeating Character Replacement.trace: AABA has 3 As and 1 B; one replacement gives AAAA, length 4.
Longest Repeating Character Replacement.pitfalls: A stale-max optimization also achieves linear time but uses a different proof; this version keeps exact window validity for clarity.

Minimum Window Substring.problem: Return the shortest substring of s containing every character of t with multiplicity, or empty. Ties keep the earliest.
Minimum Window Substring.approach: need tracks outstanding multiplicities (negative means surplus). Expand until missing becomes zero, then shrink while covering t. Each removed necessary character makes the window invalid again.
Minimum Window Substring.complexity: O(n+m+65536) time; O(65536) auxiliary counters plus output.
Minimum Window Substring.trace: ADOBEC covers ABC, then shrink; later BANC covers all three in four characters.
Minimum Window Substring.pitfalls: Repeated characters in t matter. Empty t returns empty. Characters are UTF-16 code units.
Minimum Window Substring.alternatives: Enumerate all starts and scan to coverage in O(n²) time.

Minimum Window Subsequence.problem: Return the shortest substring in which t appears as a SUBSEQUENCE in order; ties choose leftmost.
Minimum Window Subsequence.approach: For each target prefix and source prefix, store the latest possible start of a matching subsequence. Matching the next character extends the prior-prefix state; otherwise carry the current row state. Latest start gives the shortest window for a fixed end.
Minimum Window Subsequence.complexity: O(n*m) time; O(n) rolling DP space.
Minimum Window Subsequence.trace: bde matches within bcde and bdde, both length four; the first is kept.
Minimum Window Subsequence.pitfalls: Do not confuse subsequence coverage with unordered character-count coverage; Minimum Window Substring solves a different contract.

Number of Substrings Containing All Thre.problem: For a string containing only a,b,c, count substrings containing all three at least once.
Number of Substrings Containing All Thre.approach: For endpoint i, a start is valid exactly when it is at or before the earliest of the latest a/b/c positions. That contributes min(last)+1 starts.
Number of Substrings Containing All Thre.pitfalls: Before all three appear, one last index is -1 and contribution is zero. Return long for quadratic counts.

Binary Subarrays With Sum.problem: Count subarrays of binary values with sum exactly goal>=0.
Binary Subarrays With Sum.approach: Because values are nonnegative, all suffixes of a valid at-most window are valid. Subtract atMost(goal-1) from atMost(goal).
Binary Subarrays With Sum.pitfalls: Arbitrary signed values require prefix-sum hashing; this window kernel is only for nonnegative input. Zeros produce many equal-sum windows.

Count number of Nice subarrays.problem: Count subarrays containing exactly k odd values, k>=0.
Count number of Nice subarrays.approach: Map each value to parity 0/1, then count binary subarrays with sum k using the at-most difference.
Count number of Nice subarrays.complexity: O(n) time; O(n) parity array space.
Count number of Nice subarrays.trace: [1,1,2,1] and [1,2,1,1] each have three odd values.
Count number of Nice subarrays.pitfalls: Negative odd values are correctly identified by &1. The array conversion could be eliminated for O(1) auxiliary space.

Subarrays with K Different Integers.problem: Count contiguous subarrays with exactly k distinct integers.
Subarrays with K Different Integers.approach: At-most counts are easier than exactly counts: all suffixes of the longest valid at-most window qualify. The set difference between atMost(k) and atMost(k-1) leaves exactly-k windows.
Subarrays with K Different Integers.complexity: Expected O(n) time; O(min(n,k+1)) working-map space for k>=0.
Subarrays with K Different Integers.trace: [1,2,1,2] contributes six two-type windows, and [2,3] contributes one.
Subarrays with K Different Integers.pitfalls: Keep multiplicity counts, removing keys only when their count reaches zero. Return long.
